newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin says Russian economy has turned corner.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin says Russian economy has turned corner.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin told the Russian people on Friday the economy had finally turned the corner after years of industrial decline.
"The breakthrough has already happened," Yeltsin declared in a radio address marking the first anniversary of his re-election for a second and final presidential term.
"That is it. We have reached the point when it is possible for production to go up. The decline has been stopped."
The 66-year-old president did not say when or by how much the economy would grow and made clear ordinary Russians would not feel the benefit immediately.
He later told a group of regional leaders that he wanted all wage arrears to public sector workers, such as teachers and doctors, to be paid within three months.
This would build on the success of paying off a huge backlog of unpaid pensions and go hand-in-hand with promises to pay all wages owed to the military in the next two months.
Finance Minister Anatoly Chubais, sitting beside Yeltsin and at times tapping his fingers on the table., remonstrated with the president, telling him three months was not long enough to catch up.
But Yeltsin, looking flustered in brief television footage of the meeting, said: "It is possible if we all pull together."
The exchange appeared to be the first public disagreement between Yeltsin and Chubais, who was brought into the government last March to take charge of reforms.

The presidential press service denied a report by Itar-Tass news agency that Yeltsin had said he might turn to foreign leaders for help in paying off the huge wage arrears, although the agency had directly quoted him on the matter.
A recording of his remarks made by Reuters Television revealed that Yeltsin did at least make a vague reference to "external ways" of resolving the arrears problem.
"Perhaps we could seek certain ways, certain external ways. Let's give it a try," Yeltsin was filmed saying just before journalists were asked to leave the room.
In his televised remarks, Yeltsin did not say how Russia might try to raise the money nor how much was needed.

Russia has funds set aside from the World Bank to help to pay pensions and cushion the social effects of reforms, but only $300 million of the $800 million loan approved in June will be available immediately.

The government's assessments of Russia's economy are increasingly rosy. Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Wednesday that gross domestic product, the broadest measure of economic health, rose one percent in the first six months of the year.
He said it was the first rise in GDP, the value of goods and services produced, since the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.

Yeltsin, first elected in 1991, was sidelined by health problems for most of the first eight months of his second four-year term, which started a year ago. He has reaffirmed his grip on power since undergoing heart surgery last November.

"This year, I think, was the most difficult of my life, but it was also a special, unique one. I could never have imagined that a man of my age could change so much. But that is how it turned out," he said. "I can feel how I have changed."
Yeltsin said he reshuffled the government earlier this year to promote liberal reformers partly because his ill health made him realise how little time his presidency gave him to act.
"It was precisely then that I felt with particular acuteness how quickly time goes by, how much I still need to do," he said.

Yeltsin said he had a new ability to seek compromise with opponents, including the communist-led State Duma, the lower house of parliament. The Duma has blocked reforms and refused to interrupt its summer vacation to consider urgent laws.

Yeltsin discussed the impasse with the Duma's communist speaker, Gennady Seleznyov. There was no word of any breakthrough but Seleznyov said the meeting was "calm" and Tass said he was intending to take a planned holiday.
